clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group-level: Permutation Analysis of Linear Models (PALM) with threshold-free cluster enhancement and family-wise error correction for group differences in normative deviation maps between cases and controls. Individual deviations: Mann-Whitney U tests comparing total positive and negative deviations between cases and controls, with FDR correction (Benjamini-Hochberg method). Multimodal integration: Linked independent component analysis (LICA) with 20 components applied to unthresholded Z-transformed deviation maps across 4 modalities (negative faces, positive/neutral faces, shapes, anatomy) to identify shared patterns. Prediction: Logistic regression using all 20 linked ICA components to predict DBD diagnosis (McFadden's R²). Behavioral correlations: Principal component analysis (PCA) with VARIMAX rotation on aggression measures (CBCL conduct problems, oppositional defiant, ICU total, RPQ reactive and proactive) yielding one aggression factor (67% variance explained). Spearman correlations between individual modality deviations and aggression factor. Mann-Whitney U tests comparing linked ICA component scores between cases and controls. Spearman correlations between linked ICA components and aggression factor with FDR correction. Sensitivity analyses: Nonparametric partial correlations controlling for IQ, medication, internalizing symptoms, ADHD symptoms, and pubertal status.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: DBD cases showed widespread positive age-related deviations in the face-processing network (particularly amygdala, fusiform gyrus, temporal regions) suggesting maturational delay; multimodal integration of functional and anatomical deviations explained 23% variance in DBD diagnosis; the top component (component 8) involving default mode network, striatum, and amygdala was significantly associated with aggression across the whole sample.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Cases with DBD exhibited significantly more positive deviations from the normative model across all functional measures (negative faces, positive/neutral faces, shapes; all p_FDR<0.018), indicating higher age-related brain activity at the individual level, with no significant differences in negative deviations or anatomical deviations. PALM analysis revealed group-level differences in regional deviations during negative face processing, particularly in the parahippocampal gyrus/amygdala, fusiform gyrus, middle temporal gyrus, and cuneus, where cases showed more age-related activation deviations suggesting maturational delay. Deviations from positive/neutral face processing were significantly correlated with the aggression factor (ρ=0.24, p_FDR=0.036). Linked ICA identified 20 multimodal components integrating functional and anatomical deviation patterns. The 20 components together predicted 23% of the variance in DBD diagnosis (McFadden's R²=0.23, χ²=39.2, df=20, p=0.006). Component 8 was the top marker associated with aggression (ρ=-0.31, p_FDR=0.02 after controlling for internalizing symptoms; explained 9% variance in aggression factor). This component loaded most strongly on positive/neutral face and shape processing (minimal anatomical loading) and spatially encompassed the default mode network (precuneus, medial prefrontal cortex), ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens, caudate), amygdala/hippocampus, and temporal gyrus. Two components (5 and 8) showed nominal differences between cases and controls (p_uncorr=0.04 and 0.01 respectively) but did not survive FDR correction (p_FDR=0.28 and 0.20). Sensitivity analyses confirmed that correlations between component 8 and aggression remained significant when controlling for IQ (ρ=-0.30, p=0.001), medication (ρ=-0.23, p=0.01), and pubertal status (ρ=-0.28, p=0.003), and became stronger when controlling for internalizing symptoms (ρ=-0.31, p=0.001), but fell short of significance when controlling for ADHD (ρ=-0.19, p=0.05). The normative modeling approach showed superior performance compared to using raw data: linked ICA based on deviation scores showed better model fit (AIC=173.9, BIC=233.6, McFadden's R²=23%) compared to raw contrast images and JDs corrected for age and sex in-sample (AIC=182.6, BIC=248.0, R²=20%), and the components from raw data showed no associations with aggression (all p>0.09).

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Larger sample sizes would improve normative modeling and permit TD-only reference cohort; sample size insufficient to distinguish early-onset vs adolescent-onset DBD; sample size insufficient to statistically test sex differences; cross-sectional design limits inferences about neurodevelopmental trajectories (longitudinal studies needed); task combining neutral and positive faces may have diluted subtle effects; inclusion of participants with clinical CBCL scores (not formal diagnosis) increases DBD group heterogeneity
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: While this study employed a well-phenotyped sample of cases with DBD and healthy controls from a harmonized multicenter cohort, several caveats should be taken into account. First, even larger sample sizes would allow for improved normative modeling, e.g. permitting to derive normative models for TDs only. ... Second, while our data allowed investigating aggression dimensions, the sample size did not allow for a distinction between early onset and adolescent-onset DBD ... Third, our normative model was constructed based on age and sex. While the findings are suggestive of sex differences, our sample size does not allow to statistically test this. Future studies with more power should investigate this interesting topic. Fourth, given that our results are based on a cross-sectional data set, future longitudinal studies are warranted to further examine individualized brain development in DBD. Fifth, the nature of the task which included simultaneous matching of neutral and positive faces might have diluted subtle effects. ... Sixth, the inclusion of participants with clinical aggression scores in the CBCL renders the DBD group more heterogeneous

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study employed linked ICA (LICA) to integrate multimodal deviation patterns across four data types (three functional contrasts plus anatomy), treating each as a separate 'modality' with different noise characteristics. LICA provides simultaneous factorizations across modalities while linking them through a shared subject-level mixing matrix. Model order of 20 components was selected based on superior performance (AIC and BIC) compared to 30 components when predicting DBD. An aggression factor was derived using PCA with VARIMAX rotation on five aggression measures (CBCL conduct problems, oppositional defiant, ICU total, RPQ reactive and proactive), explaining 67% of variance. The normative model was trained on the whole cohort (both controls and cases) rather than controls only, due to small sample size, though sensitivity analyses on larger anatomical dataset with TD-only reference yielded similar results. The authors note that positive deviations in the amygdala during negative face processing may suggest maturational delay, as the normative model predicted gradual decrease in amygdala activity with age, but caution this interpretation may not apply to all brain regions following different trajectories and requires longitudinal validation.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a pioneering application of normative modeling to disruptive behavior disorders in youth. The study used the whole cohort (cases + controls) as the reference for normative modeling rather than controls only, justified by small sample size and validated through sensitivity analyses. The final fMRI sample (n=129: 52 controls, 77 cases) was smaller than the anatomical sample (n=127 in final or n=248 in sensitivity analysis) due to strict quality control. Medication: 66.23% of cases were on medication (39% stimulants, 20% antipsychotics, 2.6% antidepressants, 2.6% other). Comorbidity: 25.97% of cases had ADHD diagnosis. Cases had significantly lower IQ than controls (99.18±10.13 vs 108.55±10.95, p<0.001). Data were collected across 9 European sites but only 5 sites were included in final fMRI analysis to ensure minimum of 5 cases and controls per site. Cross-validation was 10-fold but it is not entirely clear if full model re-estimation occurred per fold or only out-of-sample prediction. The emotion matching task elicited the face-processing network including amygdala robustly in this sample. Visual quality control was performed by experienced rater (NH for fMRI, multiple raters for anatomical using established rating system from Backhausen et al. 2016). No systematic attrition bias was found between included and excluded participants.
